# DRAFT — Results section (English; every number is generated by `make_all.py`, see `tables/` and `figures/`)

> Status: draft for the single journal paper. Simulation-only. The Gazebo TEST family (Section R7) and the real-robot
> experiment (Section R8) are placeholders and must not be filled by hand. Notation: C1 = proposed planner; B1 = MPPI
> tuned, with the same tracker (v3) and online response model (RespModel) as C1; PGIF\* and DRA\* = our re-implementations
> of PGIF-MPPI and DRA-MPPI, sharing the same tracker, RespModel, sample budget (K = 600, T = 24) and static-obstacle
> costs; B0 = MPPI with the original tracker; DWA and log-MPPI = tuned, same tracker/RespModel. "Points" = percentage points.

## R1 Evaluation protocol (summary for the reader)

All planners command body velocities at 10 Hz. Episodes run in *fastsim*, a virtual-clock 2-D simulator that executes the
unmodified planner, tracker and perception code. A **cell** is one combination of a robot-dynamics regime (`champ`,
`champ2` = CHAMP gait in Gazebo, two identifications; `go2` = real-Go2 ranges from our measurements and the literature,
sampled per episode) and a pedestrian model (`base` or `helb`, a Helbing–Molnár-type circular potential). Five cells are
used: CHAMP/base, CHAMP2/base, Go2/base, CHAMP2/Helbing, Go2/Helbing. The primary metric is **success = goal reached with
no collision of any kind**. The design (C1 and all six baselines) was frozen with SHA-256 hashes before validation;
the TEST analysis was pre-registered (`audit/PREREG_TEST.md`), and TEST was run once, from a read-only snapshot of the
frozen code, with the hashes checked before every cell. The TEST set consists of the first 1000 generated worlds with
people at or above seed 100000 (seeds 100000–101386); each world is run once in each of the five cells for each of the seven
planners (35 000 episodes; 0 infrastructure exclusions). The primary family has three comparisons (C1 vs B1, PGIF\*, DRA\*).
Each is tested on the world-level paired difference d_w (C1 − X, averaged over the five cells) with a two-sided
sign-flip permutation test (200 000 flips) and a percentile bootstrap CI over worlds (10 000), with Holm correction.

## R2 Main result (fastsim TEST, Table T1, Figure F1, Table T2)

C1 had the highest success in every cell (Table T1). Pooled over cells, success was **85.3 %** for C1 (Wilson 95 % CI 84.3–86.2;
world-bootstrap 83.7–86.7), 82.6 % for DRA\*, 80.3 % for PGIF\*, 79.1 % for DWA, 78.3 % for B1, 77.9 % for log-MPPI and
68.9 % for B0 (n = 5000 episodes per planner).

All three pre-registered comparisons favoured C1 (Table T2):

| Comparison | Δ (points) | 95 % CI | p (perm.) | p (Holm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 − B1 | +6.96 | [+5.68, +8.26] | 5e-6 | 1.5e-5 |
| C1 − PGIF\* | +4.98 | [+3.76, +6.24] | 5e-6 | 1.5e-5 |
| C1 − DRA\* | +2.66 | [+1.52, +3.80] | 5e-6 | 1.5e-5 |

(p = 5e-6 is the smallest value the 200 000-flip test can return.) By the pre-registered rule ("C1 better than X only if
p_Holm < 0.05 and Δ > 0"), C1 is better than all three baselines on fastsim TEST. Descriptively (no test was registered),
C1 exceeded B0 by +16.36 points, DWA by +6.20 and log-MPPI by +7.40. Most of the gap to B0 is due to the tracker v3 and the
RespModel, which every tuned baseline also uses: B1 − B0 = 78.3 − 68.9 = 9.4 points.

## R3 Where the advantage comes from: cells (Table T3, Figure F2)

The per-cell paired differences were positive in all 15 cell × baseline combinations (smallest +0.8 points), but their size
depended strongly on the condition:

- **vs B1**: +7.9 (CHAMP/base), +12.3 (CHAMP2/base), +6.1 (Go2/base), +6.7 (CHAMP2/Helbing), all Holm ≤ 2.6e-5 (exact McNemar,
  Holm over 15); in **Go2/Helbing** +1.8 (61 vs 43 discordant pairs, p = 0.095, Holm 0.48).
- **vs PGIF\***: +6.7, +8.0 and +6.1 in the three base-crowd cells (Holm ≤ 8.4e-5); +2.7 in CHAMP2/Helbing (Holm 0.28) and +1.4 in
  Go2/Helbing (Holm 0.86).
- **vs DRA\***: significant only in **CHAMP2/base** (+5.9, 122 vs 63, Holm 1.4e-4). CHAMP/base +1.7 (Holm 0.86), Go2/base +1.4
  (Holm 0.86), CHAMP2/Helbing +3.5 (p = 0.009, Holm 0.064) and Go2/Helbing +0.8 (48 vs 40, Holm 0.86) were not significant.

Thus the C1 advantage is large when the robot is slow relative to pedestrians (CHAMP dynamics, commands clipped at 0.3 m/s)
and the base crowd is used, and small or absent when the robot is fast (Go2 regime) and pedestrians follow the Helbing-type
model. Against DRA\* it is established only pooled and in one cell. No cell changed sign.

## R4 Failure modes (Table T4, Figure F4)

Almost all failures were collisions with people. Pooled over the five cells, the person-collision rate was 13.8 % for C1
versus 16.7 % (DRA\*), 19.0 % (PGIF\*), 20.5 % (B1), 20.6 % (DWA), 20.8 % (log-MPPI) and 30.8 % (B0). Static-obstacle
collisions (≤ 0.3 %), stuck episodes (≤ 0.6 %), timeouts (≤ 0.7 %) and no-path episodes (≤ 0.04 %) were rare for all planners;
C1 had 0.12 % static collisions, 0.44 % stuck, 0.32 % timeouts. Mean time to goal over *successful* episodes was 59.0 s for C1,
58.5 s for DRA\*, 56.0 s for PGIF\* and 70.8 s for B1 (these means are conditional on success and therefore over different
episode subsets; they are descriptive only). The fastsim at-fault flag marks 527 of C1's 692 person collisions; we do not
interpret this flag (see Limitations).

## R5 Static-only arm (Table T5, Figure F4 right)

To check that the pedestrian layer does not degrade static-obstacle navigation, a pre-registered secondary arm used all
387 seeds in the TEST range that contain no people (3 regimes, 1161 episodes per planner). All planners succeeded in
96–99.5 % of episodes, with no static collisions except B0 (0.09 %); every other failure was "stuck". C1 reached
96.9 % (Wilson 95.7–97.8) versus 97.8 % for B1: Δ = −0.95 points [−1.55, −0.34]. The pre-registered non-inferiority criterion
(lower bound > −2 points) was met, but the deficit is real: C1 got stuck more often (3.1 % vs 2.2 %). DWA (99.5 %) and B0
(99.0 %) were the best planners in static worlds (C1 − DWA −2.58 [−3.96, −1.38]; C1 − B0 −2.07 [−3.19, −1.03]; descriptive).
We attribute this, without a controlled test, to tracker v3 retaining or creating person tracks on static clutter, which makes
C1 wait; the same mechanism produced the ghost tracks observed in Gazebo (Limitations).

## R6 Ablation and simplification (Table T6, Figure F5)

In a development confirmation round (seeds 1000–1499, 348 worlds × 3 base-crowd cells, run once) removing one component at a
time from C1 gave: tracker v3 → v2 −5.8 points [−8.7, −3.0] (Holm 0.0014); removing the evasive primitive samples −4.2
[−6.7, −1.7] (Holm 0.029); replacing the discounted geometric risk with the plain people cost −2.2 [−4.6, +0.1] (Holm 1);
removing the temperature fix −1.1, the time discount −0.7, and the RespModel −0.4 (all Holm 1). Only the tracker and the
evasive samples are individually shown to matter. In the next round (seeds 1500–1999, 357 worlds × 5 cells) we tested,
under a pre-registered non-inferiority rule (margin −2 points), three simpler variants: MPPI + primitives without
(−5.66 [−7.79, −3.59]) and with RespModel (−5.66 [−7.62, −3.70]), and C1 without temperature fix, discount and RespModel
(−0.84 [−2.69, +0.95]). None met the rule, so the full C1 was frozen. The geometric risk and the temperature fix appear to be
partly interchangeable (removing both costs ~5.7 points, removing either alone ≤ 2.2), but this was not tested directly.

## R7 Replication across seed sets (Table T10, Figure F3)

The same comparison was repeated on five disjoint sets of worlds with people. Recomputed with the TEST procedure:

| Seed set | Worlds | C1 − B1 | C1 − PGIF\* | C1 − DRA\* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 confirmation (300–799) | 356 | +5.73 [+3.60, +7.92] | – | – |
| R2 confirmation (1000–1499) | 348 | +6.61 [+4.60, +8.62] | +5.23 [+3.22, +7.36] | +3.16 [+1.21, +5.17] (Holm 0.0018) |
| R3 confirmation (1500–1999) | 357 | +7.17 [+5.10, +9.36] | +6.05 [+3.92, +8.18] | +2.80 [+0.90, +4.65] (Holm 0.0043) |
| VAL (2000–2399) | 315 | +9.08 [+6.98, +11.17] | +6.22 [+4.06, +8.32] | +4.51 [+2.47, +6.54] |
| **TEST (≥ 100000)** | 1000 | **+6.96 [+5.68, +8.26]** | **+4.98 [+3.76, +6.24]** | **+2.66 [+1.52, +3.80]** |

The sign and approximate size of each gap replicated in every set. R1–R3 were development confirmation rounds (each run once
after the candidate had been locked) and VAL was a pre-registered validation; only TEST is confirmatory, and the sets are not
pooled. The gap to DRA\* is consistently the smallest (2.7–4.5 points).

## R8 Computation time (Table T7)

On the development laptop (numpy), C1 needed 8.6 ms per control step on average (p99 10.9 ms), comparable to B1 (8.7 / 12.1 ms),
PGIF\* (9.1 / 11.1 ms) and DRA\* (9.2 / 12.7 ms, plus a one-off 205 ms table construction at the first step). With the optional C
kernels: 7.5 ms (p99 9.6 ms). In the Gazebo smoke test the measured C1 step time was 7.5 ms median, 15.4 ms p95, 48 ms max
(16 343 steps), and the command period stayed at 0.101 s median / 0.108 s p95, within the 100 ms control period. Timing on the
robot's onboard computer (Jetson Orin) has not been measured.

## R9 Simulator fidelity and an independent body model (Tables T8, T9)

*Dynamics (T8).* Re-identifying the CHAMP gait from Gazebo logs showed that the apparent 0.29 m/s "saturation" is the command
clipping of the CHAMP gait configuration (0.30/0.25/0.50) plus a ~0.053 m/s backward drift while stepping. The resulting `champ2`
model predicts 2-s open-loop motion better than the original `champ` model (mean error 0.062 vs 0.088 m; ideal v = cmd 0.169 m).
Two official Isaac Lab Go2 policies track forward commands up to 1 m/s with gain ≈ 1 (gain 0.99 [0.97, 1.00] at 0.4–0.6 m/s for the
rough policy), confirming that the 0.3 m/s limit belongs to CHAMP, not to the Go2 body.

*Closed-loop fidelity (T9-A).* On 8 development office tasks and 12 planners, fastsim success rates ranked planners like 960
Gazebo episodes with Spearman ρ = 0.90 (champ regime) and 0.59 (champ2). The difference (+0.31, task-bootstrap 95 % CI
[−0.13, +0.42]) is inconclusive; most of the agreement comes from separating learned/pure-pursuit planners from the MPPI family.
We therefore report all three regimes as robustness conditions and do not call any of them "the Gazebo model".

*Isaac cross-check (T9-B/C).* Replacing the fastsim body by the Isaac Lab rough-terrain policy with observation noise
(rays, crowd and tracker unchanged) on 100 development worlds reproduced the fastsim ranking of five planners
(Kendall τ = 1.00 vs fastsim go2 and champ, 0.80 vs champ2). C1 succeeded in 83/100 vs 75/100 for B1 (McNemar +20/−12, p = 0.22;
the pilot was not powered). In a later deterministic re-run on the same worlds, C1 succeeded in 87/100 vs 73/100 for B1 (+20/−6,
p = 0.009; exploratory, not pre-registered). Isaac adds a failure mode absent from fastsim — falls (6 for C1, 5 for B1 in the pilot);
they were traced to the learned policy's weakness at slow reverse/turning commands, which the shared tracker's waiting behaviour
produces more often, and an optional command shaper removed them (0/200), at a cost of 5–8 points (n.s.) in fastsim go2.

## Suggested one-paragraph summary (for the abstract; update after R10/R11)
On a pre-registered fastsim test of 1000 unseen worlds × 5 dynamics/crowd conditions (35 000 episodes), C1 reached the goal
without collision in 85.3 % of episodes, versus 78.3 % for tuned MPPI with the same perception (+7.0 points [5.7, 8.3]), 80.3 % for
a PGIF-MPPI re-implementation (+5.0 [3.8, 6.2]) and 82.6 % for a DRA-MPPI re-implementation (+2.7 [1.5, 3.8]); all Holm-adjusted
p < 1e-4. The advantage was replicated on four further disjoint seed sets, but it is condition-dependent: against DRA-MPPI it is
significant in only one of five conditions, and with a fast robot and Helbing-type pedestrians C1 is statistically
indistinguishable from all three baselines. In static-only worlds C1 is non-inferior to tuned MPPI but 0.95 points worse.
